plan.report_shape: Provide three concise sections: definitions for 401 and 403, then a clear rule for when to return 401 instead of 403 (and vice versa), each backed by the cited HTTP RFC language and header/behavior expectations.

research_limitations: Direct RFC 9110 normative quotation for the specific `401 Unauthorized` definition was not retrieved in the provided sources; only an RFC-editor pointer to the (now obsolete) RFC 7235 authentication section is available, while the captured normative details about `WWW-Authenticate` come from MDN and a non-RFC explainer [https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7235, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate].

Whether `WWW-Authenticate` is strictly required in *every* 401 case per RFC 9110 text (vs commonly required practice) cannot be confirmed from the provided sources; one external discussion reports real-world cases where 401 is missing `WWW-Authenticate` (but this is not normative RFC text) [https://community.developers.lseg.com/discussion/52787/missing-www-authenticate-header-when-receiving-401-responses].

The provided sources do not include the exact RFC 9110 (sections 15.5.2 and 15.5.4) text that explicitly states the 401-vs-403 decision criteria and behavioral requirements; IANA only provides the section mapping, not the detailed RFC wording. [https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes]

The sources include MDN guidance for `WWW-Authenticate` with 401 and a definition for 403, but the specific statement about what the server should do *not* do in 403 responses (e.g., “do not include `WWW-Authenticate` / do not issue an auth challenge”) is not directly quoted from RFC 9110 in the provided results; it is implied via MDN semantics rather than explicitly evidenced in RFC language. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
